text: The TCP/IP protocol suite stands for Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol.
TCP/IP is a protocol suite used in the Internet today.
A protocol suite is a set of protocols organized in different layers.
TCP/IP is a hierarchical protocol.
TCP/IP is made up of interactive modules.
Each module in the TCP/IP suite provides a specific functionality.
In a hierarchical protocol, each upper level protocol is supported by services from lower level protocols.
The original TCP/IP protocol suite was defined as four software layers.
The original four software layers of TCP/IP were built upon the hardware.
Today, TCP/IP is conceptualized as a five-layer model.
A router is involved in only three layers of the TCP/IP model.
There is no transport layer in a router as long as it is used only for routing.
There is no application layer in a router as long as it is used only for routing.
A router is always involved in exactly one network layer.
A router is involved in n combinations of link and physical layers, where n is the number of links connected to it.
Each link connected to a router may use its own data-link protocol.
Each link connected to a router may use its own physical protocol.
A router can receive a packet from one link based on one pair of protocols and deliver it to another link based on another pair.
A link-layer switch in a link is involved in only two layers.
The two layers a link-layer switch is involved in are the data-link and physical layers.
Connections on a switch within the same link use only one set of protocols.
Unlike a router, a link-layer switch is involved in only one data-link layer and one physical layer.
The physical layer is responsible for carrying individual bits in a frame across a link.
The physical layer is the lowest level in the TCP/IP protocol suite.
Communication between two devices at the physical layer is a logical communication.
There is a hidden transmission media layer under the physical layer.
Two devices are connected by a transmission medium, such as cable or air.
The transmission medium does not carry bits directly.
The transmission medium carries electrical or optical signals.
Bits received in a frame from the data-link layer are transformed into signals for transmission.
The logical unit of communication between two physical layers in two devices is a bit.
There are several protocols that transform a bit into an electrical or optical signal.
An internet is made up of several links connected by routers.
Links making up an internet can be LANs or WANs.
A datagram can travel from host to destination through overlapping sets of links.
Routers are responsible for choosing the best links for a datagram to travel.
When a router determines the next link, the data-link layer takes the datagram to move it across the link.
The data-link layer is responsible for moving the packet through the link.
A link can be a wired LAN with a link-layer switch.
A link can be a wireless LAN, wired WAN, or wireless WAN.
Different protocols can be used with any type of link.
TCP/IP does not define any specific protocol for the data-link layer.
TCP/IP supports all standard and proprietary data-link protocols.
Any protocol that can carry a datagram through a link suffices for the network layer.
The data-link layer encapsulates a datagram into a packet called a frame.
Each link-layer protocol may provide a different service.
Some link-layer protocols provide complete error detection and correction.
Some link-layer protocols provide only error correction.
The network layer creates a connection between the source computer and the destination computer.
Communication at the network layer is host-to-host.
Routers in the path are responsible for choosing the best route for each packet.
The network layer is responsible for host-to-host communication and routing the packet through possible routes.
Separating routing tasks from the transport layer into the network layer allows the use of fewer protocols on routers.
The main protocol in the Internet network layer is the Internet Protocol (IP).
IP defines the format of the network layer packet, called a datagram.
IP defines the format and structure of addresses used in the network layer.
IP is responsible for routing a packet from its source to its destination.
Routing is achieved by each router forwarding the datagram to the next router in its path.
IP is a connectionless protocol.
IP provides no flow control services.
IP provides no error control services.
IP provides no congestion control services.
If flow, error, or congestion control are required, the application must rely on the transport-layer protocol.
The network layer includes unicast (one-to-one) routing protocols.
The network layer includes multicast (one-to-many) routing protocols.
A routing protocol creates forwarding tables for routers to help in the routing process.
A routing protocol itself does not take part in the actual routing of packets.
The network layer has auxiliary protocols that help IP in its delivery and routing tasks.
The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) helps IP report problems when routing a packet.
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) helps IP in multitasking.
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) helps IP get the network-layer address for a host.
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) helps IP find the link-layer address of a host or router.
The logical connection at the transport layer is end-to-end.
The transport layer at the source host gets the message from the application layer.
The transport layer encapsulates messages into a packet called a segment or a user datagram.
The transport layer provides services to the application layer.
The transport layer should be independent of the application layer.
Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a connection-oriented protocol.
TCP establishes a logical connection between transport layers before transferring data.
User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is a connectionless protocol that transmits datagrams without a logical connection.
Two models have been devised to define computer network operations: the TCP/IP protocol suite and the OSI model.
A protocol defines the rules that the sender, receiver, and all intermediate devices need to follow to communicate effectively.
When communication is simple, only one simple protocol may be needed.
When communication is complex, the task may need to be divided between different layers.
Protocol layering refers to having a specific protocol at each divided layer of communication.
Protocol layering enables a complex communication task to be divided into several smaller and simpler tasks.
Modularity in protocol layering means that each layer is independent.
A layer can be defined as a black box with inputs and outputs, without concern for how inputs are changed to outputs.
One advantage of protocol layering is that it allows the separation of services from their implementation.
In a layered architecture, a layer must be able to receive services from the lower layer and provide services to the upper layer.
Protocol layering allows intermediate systems to use only necessary layers, avoiding the complexity of end systems.
The first principle of protocol layering dictates that each layer must perform two opposite tasks for bidirectional communication.
The second principle of protocol layering dictates that the two objects under each corresponding layer at both sites should be identical.
Logical connections refer to the imaginary, layer-to-layer communication between peer layers at different sites.
The TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) protocol suite is currently used in the Internet.
TCP/IP is a hierarchical protocol made up of interactive modules, each providing specific functionality.
In a hierarchical protocol, each upper-level protocol is supported by services provided by lower-level protocols.
The original TCP/IP protocol suite was defined as four software layers built upon hardware.
Today, TCP/IP is generally conceptualized as a five-layer model.
The five layers of the TCP/IP protocol suite are physical, data-link, network, transport, and application.
A source host creates a message in the application layer and sends it down through all five TCP/IP layers.
A destination host receives communication at the physical layer and delivers it up through all five layers.
A router is involved in only the physical, data-link, and network layers.
A router used strictly for routing has no transport or application layer.
A router is always involved in exactly one network layer.
A router is involved in multiple combinations of link and physical layers, depending on the number of links it connects to.
Each link connected to a router may use its own distinct data-link or physical protocol.
A link-layer switch operates only in the data-link and physical layers.
Connections on a single link-layer switch use only one set of protocols.
The duty of the application, transport, and network layers is considered end-to-end.
The domain of duty of the top three TCP/IP layers is the entire internet.
The duty of the data-link and physical layers is considered hop-to-hop.
A hop in network terminology can refer to a host or a router.
The domain of duty of the bottom two TCP/IP layers is the specific link.
Data units in the top three layers should not be altered by any router or link-layer switch.
In the bottom two layers, packets created by the host can be changed by routers, but not by link-layer switches.
Identical objects exist between two hops at the network layer because a router may need to fragment the packet.
The physical layer is responsible for carrying individual bits in a frame across a link.
Communication between two devices at the physical layer is a logical communication over the transmission media.
The transmission medium serves as a hidden layer under the physical layer.
Transmission media carry electrical or optical signals, not literal bits.
Bits received from the data-link layer are transformed into signals by protocols in the physical layer.
The logical unit of communication between two physical layers is a bit.
An internet consists of overlapping sets of links connected by routers.
Routers are responsible for choosing the best link for a packet to travel next.
The data-link layer is responsible for taking a datagram from the network layer and moving it across the chosen link.
TCP/IP does not define a specific protocol for the data-link layer, supporting all standard and proprietary protocols.
Any protocol that can carry a datagram through a link suffices for the network layer.
The data-link layer encapsulates a network-layer datagram into a packet known as a frame.
Some link-layer protocols provide complete error detection and correction, while others provide only error detection.
The network layer creates a host-to-host connection between the source and destination computers.
The network layer is responsible for routing a packet through possible routes using intermediate routers.
Separating routing duties into the network layer allows routers to function without needing transport or application layers.
The Internet Protocol (IP) is the main protocol in the TCP/IP network layer.
IP defines the format of the network-layer packet, which is called a datagram.
IP defines the format and structure of the global addresses used in the network layer.
Routing is achieved by each router forwarding an IP datagram to the next router in its path.
IP is a connectionless protocol that provides no flow, error, or congestion control services.
If flow or error control is required, an application must rely on the transport-layer protocol.
The network layer includes unicast and multicast routing protocols that create forwarding tables for routers.
The Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) helps IP report problems that occur when routing packets.
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) helps IP manage multicasting group memberships.
The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) helps IP obtain a network-layer address for a host.
The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) helps IP find the link-layer address of a node when its network-layer address is known.
The logical connection at the transport layer is an end-to-end connection between hosts.
The transport layer encapsulates messages from the application layer into packets called segments or user datagrams.
The transport layer is responsible for delivering a message from an application program on the source to the corresponding program on the destination.
The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a connection-oriented transport protocol that establishes a logical connection before transferring data.
TCP creates a logical pipe for transferring a continuous stream of bytes between two endpoints.
TCP provides flow control to prevent the sender from overwhelming the receiver's data rate.
TCP provides error control to guarantee that segments arrive without error, resending corrupted ones.
TCP utilizes congestion control to reduce segment loss due to network congestion.
The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) is a simple, connectionless transport protocol that transmits independent user datagrams.
UDP has minimal overhead because it does not provide flow, error, or congestion control.
The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a newer transport protocol designed to handle multimedia applications.
Communication at the application layer is a logical process-to-process exchange of messages.
The application layer in the Internet utilizes many predefined protocols, like HTTP, SMTP, and FTP.
The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is the standard vehicle for accessing the World Wide Web.
The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) is the primary protocol for electronic mail services.
The File Transfer Protocol (FTP) facilitates transferring files between hosts.
Terminal Network (TELNET) and Secure Shell (SSH) are protocols used for remote site access.
The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is used by administrators to monitor and manage the Internet.
The Domain Name System (DNS) is utilized by other protocols to resolve domain names into network-layer IP addresses.
Encapsulation occurs exclusively at the source host as data moves down the TCP/IP layers.
At the application layer, the exchanged data is referred to as a message, normally lacking headers or trailers.
The transport layer adds a header containing source and destination application identifiers to the message payload.
The network layer adds a header containing global source and destination host addresses to the transport-layer payload.
The data-link layer adds a header containing local link-layer addresses for the host or next-hop router.
At a router, both decapsulation and encapsulation occur as packets move between different links.
A router decapsulates a datagram from an incoming frame and passes it to its network layer for inspection.
The router's network layer consults its forwarding table to determine the next hop based on the destination address.
After determining the next hop, a router encapsulates the unmodified datagram into a new link-layer frame for transmission.
At the destination host, each layer decapsulates the packet, checks for errors, and delivers the payload upwards.
The TCP/IP protocol suite typically uses four pairs of addresses, as the physical layer handles raw bits that have no address.
Application layer addresses often take the form of readable names, such as URLs or e-mail addresses.
Transport layer addresses are known as port numbers, which identify specific application processes.
Port numbers act as local addresses to distinguish among multiple concurrent programs on the same host.
Network-layer addresses are global and uniquely define a device's connection to the entire Internet.
Link-layer addresses, often called MAC addresses, are local and define a specific node within a single LAN or WAN.
Multiplexing at a source means a lower-layer protocol can encapsulate packets originating from several different higher-layer protocols.
Demultiplexing at a destination means a lower-layer protocol can decapsulate and route payloads to the correct higher-layer protocol.
To support multiplexing, protocol headers must include a field identifying which higher-level protocol the payload belongs to.
The transport layer can multiplex messages from multiple application protocols like HTTP, DNS, and FTP.
The network layer IP can multiplex segments from TCP, user datagrams from UDP, and packets from ICMP or IGMP.
The data-link layer frame may carry payloads coming from IP or directly from auxiliary protocols like ARP.
The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) created the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model.
An open system allows communication between different computer systems regardless of their underlying architecture.
The OSI model is not a protocol itself, but a layered framework for designing network architectures.
The OSI model consists of seven distinct but related layers to structure network communication.
The session and presentation layers of the OSI model are absent from the TCP/IP protocol suite.
The application layer in the TCP/IP suite generally encompasses the functions of the application, presentation, and session layers of the OSI model.
The ISO is a multinational body dedicated to establishing worldwide international standards.
The OSI model was first introduced in the late 1970s.
The application layer is the highest layer in the TCP/IP suite and provides services directly to the user.
The application layer relies exclusively on services provided by the transport layer.
The payload at the transport layer is exactly the message generated by the application layer.
The payload at the network layer is exactly the segment or datagram generated by the transport layer.
The payload at the data-link layer is exactly the datagram generated by the network layer.
The transport layer header contains information needed for end-to-end delivery of the message.
A network-layer IP address specifies the final destination, while a link-layer address specifies the immediate next hop.
A router acts as an internetworking device, utilizing the network layer to forward packets across different networks.
The TCP/IP model has proven more successful in practical implementation than the OSI model.
The term 'hop' in hop-to-hop delivery refers to moving data across a single link between adjacent nodes.
A frame is specifically the name of the packet structure used at the data-link layer.
Routing protocols create dynamic forwarding tables to assist IP in directing datagrams.
The process of moving a datagram into a frame is an example of encapsulation.
The process of removing a datagram from an incoming frame is an example of decapsulation.
End systems, such as source and destination hosts, require all five layers of the TCP/IP suite to function.
Every layer in a network model must have a predefined structure for its headers and data.
The physical layer translates logical bits into physical signals suitable for the transmission medium.
The transport layer sits between the application layer above and the network layer below in the TCP/IP suite.
The network layer sits between the transport layer above and the data-link layer below in the TCP/IP suite.
The data-link layer sits between the network layer above and the physical layer below in the TCP/IP suite.
A connection-oriented transport protocol ensures data arrives in order.
A connectionless transport protocol allows data chunks to be sent independently without a formal connection setup.
The domain of operation for the network layer is the entire end-to-end path through multiple networks.
A link-layer address changes at each hop as a packet moves from router to router.
A network-layer address generally remains constant as a packet moves from its source to its final destination.
A port number address remains constant to identify the application processes engaged in communication.
The network layer header includes both the source host IP address and the destination host IP address.
The transport layer header includes both the source port number and the destination port number.
A switch operating at the data-link layer forwards frames based on their link-layer destination addresses.
A router forwards packets based on their network-layer destination addresses.
The TCP/IP application layer does not provide services to any other protocols within the suite.
New application protocols can be easily added as long as they interface correctly with the transport layer.
The flexibility of protocol layering enables different physical transmission media to be used without changing upper layer software.
Error checking at the destination host during decapsulation ensures data integrity before handing it to the application.
The TCP protocol includes a sequence numbering system to enable reassembly of a byte stream.
UDP is preferred for applications where speed is more critical than guaranteed delivery.
The conceptual model of TCP/IP simplifies the understanding of complex internetwork communications.
Information can exist in various forms such as voice, picture, numeric data, or characters.
To be transmitted across a network, information needs to be transformed into electromagnetic signals.
Data in computer networks can be broadly classified as either analog or digital.
Analog data refers to information that is continuous and takes on continuous values.
Digital data refers to information that has discrete states and takes on discrete values.
The human voice is a classic example of analog data because sound waves are continuous.
Data stored in the memory of a computer in the form of 0s and 1s is an example of digital data.
Electromagnetic signals used for transmission can also be either analog or digital.
An analog signal has infinitely many levels of intensity over a period of time.
A digital signal can have only a limited number of defined values, often simply 1 and 0.
Periodic signals complete a specific pattern within a measurable time frame called a period.
Nonperiodic signals change constantly without exhibiting a pattern or cycle that repeats over time.
In data communications, we most commonly utilize periodic analog signals and nonperiodic digital signals.
A periodic analog signal can be classified as either simple or composite.
A simple periodic analog signal, such as a sine wave, cannot be decomposed into simpler signals.
A composite periodic analog signal is composed of multiple independent sine waves.
The sine wave is the most fundamental form of a periodic analog signal.
A sine wave is mathematically characterized by three parameters: peak amplitude, frequency, and phase.
Peak amplitude is the absolute value of the highest intensity of a signal, which is proportional to the energy it carries.
Period (T) is the amount of time, usually measured in seconds, a signal needs to complete one full cycle.
Frequency (f) is the number of periods or cycles that a signal completes in exactly one second.
Frequency and period are mathematical inverses of each other, defined by the equations f = 1/T and T = 1/f.
While period is formally expressed in seconds, frequency is expressed in Hertz (Hz).
Frequency represents the rate of change of a signal with respect to time.
If the value of a signal changes over a very short span of time, its frequency is considered high.
If the value of a signal changes gradually over a long span of time, its frequency is considered low.
If a signal does not change its value at all over time, its frequency is zero.
If a signal changes its value instantaneously, its frequency is theoretically infinite.
Phase describes the position of the waveform relative to time zero.
Phase is typically measured in degrees or radians.
A phase shift of 360 degrees corresponds to a time shift of exactly one complete period.
Wavelength is the physical distance a simple signal can travel in one period.
Wavelength depends on both the frequency of the signal and the physical medium through which it travels.
Wavelength is calculated by multiplying the propagation speed of the medium by the period of the signal.
A time-domain plot graphs the changes in signal amplitude with respect to time.
A frequency-domain plot graphs the peak amplitude values of a signal with respect to its frequency.
A complete sine wave in the time domain is represented by a single spike in the frequency domain.
A single-frequency sine wave is generally not useful for data communications because it carries little information.
To effectively communicate data, we need to send a composite signal.
According to Fourier analysis, any composite signal is simply a combination of simple sine waves with varying frequencies, amplitudes, and phases.
If a composite signal is periodic, its Fourier decomposition yields a series of discrete frequency signals.
If a composite signal is nonperiodic, its Fourier decomposition yields a continuous combination of sine waves.
The bandwidth of a composite signal is the mathematical difference between its highest and lowest frequency components.
A digital signal typically represents data as a sequence of discrete voltage levels.
In a basic digital signal, a 1 can be encoded as a positive voltage and a 0 as zero voltage.
A digital signal can be designed to have more than two levels to carry more bits per signal change.
If a digital signal has L discrete levels, each level needs log2(L) bits to be properly represented.
The bit rate is the number of bits successfully sent in one second, expressed in bits per second (bps).
The bit length is the physical distance one single bit occupies on the transmission medium.
Bit length is calculated as the propagation speed of the medium multiplied by the bit duration.
A digital signal is fundamentally a composite analog signal with an infinite bandwidth.
The fundamental frequency of a theoretical digital signal is zero, and its highest frequency is infinity.
Baseband transmission involves sending a digital signal directly over a channel without changing it to an analog signal.
Baseband transmission requires a low-pass channel, which is a channel with a bandwidth that begins at zero.
A theoretical low-pass channel with infinite bandwidth allows the exact, sharp shape of a digital signal to be preserved.
In reality, no physical transmission channel has an infinite bandwidth; all channels are band-limited.
Baseband transmission over a band-limited channel forces the receiver to accept an approximation of the original digital signal.
In baseband transmission, the required bandwidth of the channel is directly proportional to the intended bit rate.
Broadband transmission (or modulation) involves changing a digital signal into an analog signal for transmission.
Broadband transmission uses a bandpass channel, which is a channel whose bandwidth does not start from zero.
If the only available channel is a bandpass channel, a digital signal cannot be sent directly and must be modulated.
Signals traveling through any physical transmission media are not perfect and will always experience impairment.
Transmission impairment means the signal received at the end of the medium is degraded compared to the signal sent at the beginning.
The three primary causes of transmission impairment are attenuation, distortion, and noise.
Attenuation refers specifically to a loss of signal energy over distance.
As a signal travels, it loses energy because it must overcome the electrical or optical resistance of the medium.
Amplifiers are devices placed along a transmission path to compensate for attenuation by boosting the signal.
The decibel (dB) is a logarithmic unit used to measure the relative strengths of two signals or one signal at two points.
A negative decibel value indicates signal attenuation, while a positive decibel value indicates signal amplification.
Distortion implies that the signal has changed its form or shape during transmission.
Distortion typically occurs in composite signals made of many different frequency components.
Different frequency components of a composite signal often travel at slightly different propagation speeds through a medium.
These differences in propagation speeds cause phase shifts among frequencies, resulting in delay distortion.
Noise is any unwanted external signal that inserts itself into and corrupts the transmitted signal.
Common types of noise include thermal noise, induced noise, crosstalk, and impulse noise.
Thermal noise is generated by the random microscopic motion of electrons in a wire, creating a persistent background signal.
Induced noise occurs when external sources like motors or appliances act as transmitting antennas, and the medium acts as a receiving antenna.
Crosstalk is the unwanted electrical coupling between adjacent wires, where one wire induces a signal into the other.
Impulse noise is a sudden, highly energetic spike originating from events like lightning strikes or power line surges.
The Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) is the ratio of average signal power to average noise power.
A high SNR is desirable as it indicates the signal is much stronger than the background noise.
A low SNR indicates the signal is heavily corrupted by noise, making data extraction difficult.
Because SNR deals with a ratio of powers that can span large ranges, it is usually described in decibels (SNRdB).
The data rate limit dictates the absolute maximum speed data can be sent over a specific channel in bits per second.
The theoretical data rate depends heavily on the available bandwidth, the number of signal levels, and the channel's noise level.
The Nyquist bit rate formula determines the theoretical maximum bit rate exclusively for a noiseless channel.
The Nyquist formula defines maximum bit rate as 2 * Bandwidth * log2(L), where L is the number of discrete signal levels.
While increasing signal levels (L) increases the theoretical bit rate, it makes the system more susceptible to noise errors.
The Shannon capacity formula determines the theoretical highest data rate limit for a realistic, noisy channel.
The Shannon capacity defines the maximum data rate as Bandwidth * log2(1 + SNR).
The Shannon capacity sets an upper limit on the data rate that cannot be exceeded regardless of how many signal levels are used.
In engineering practice, Shannon's capacity dictates the upper limit, while Nyquist's formula determines how many signal levels are needed to achieve it.
Bandwidth expressed in Hertz refers to the physical range of frequencies a channel can successfully pass.
Bandwidth expressed in bits per second refers to the theoretical maximum number of bits a link can transmit in one second.
Throughput is a practical measure of how fast data can actually be pushed through a network under real-world conditions.
Throughput is always less than or equal to the link's theoretical bandwidth.
Latency (or delay) measures the total time required for an entire message to arrive at its destination after the first bit leaves the source.
Total latency is the sum of propagation time, transmission time, queuing time, and processing delay.
Propagation time is the time it takes for a single bit's electromagnetic wave to travel from source to destination.
Propagation time is calculated by dividing the physical distance by the propagation speed of the specific medium.
Transmission time is the time required for a network interface to push all the bits of a message onto the wire.
Transmission time is calculated by dividing the total message size by the bandwidth of the channel.
Queuing time is the variable amount of time a packet spends waiting in router or switch buffers before being processed.
Processing delay is the time a router takes to inspect a packet's header, check for errors, and determine its outgoing routing path.
The bandwidth-delay product conceptually represents the maximum number of bits that can fill a link at any given time.
The bandwidth-delay product is calculated mathematically by multiplying the link's bandwidth by its propagation time.
To fully utilize the capacity of a long-distance link, a sender must keep a number of unacknowledged bits in transit equal to the bandwidth-delay product.
Jitter is a critical issue in real-time multimedia communications, arising from inconsistent delays.
Jitter occurs when consecutive packets of an audio or video stream experience varying queuing times, causing them to arrive unevenly.
Attenuation in decibels can be calculated using the formula 10 * log10(P2/P1), where P1 is the input power and P2 is the output power.
Any composite signal can be visually represented and analyzed in both the time domain and the frequency domain.
The frequency domain is often much more compact and useful for analyzing signals containing a large number of varying frequencies.
In a standard frequency-domain plot, the horizontal axis represents frequency while the vertical axis represents peak amplitude.
A signal that maintains a constant voltage over time has a frequency of zero and is known as a DC (direct current) signal.
An analog signal is defined as band-limited if it contains a finite range of frequencies rather than an infinite spectrum.
An infinite bandwidth is theoretically required to perfectly transmit a digital signal with perfectly vertical rising and falling edges.
The Fourier series is a mathematical tool that decomposes a periodic composite signal into its discrete sine wave components.
The Fourier transform is a mathematical tool that decomposes a nonperiodic composite signal into a continuous frequency spectrum.
The time and frequency domains are not mutually exclusive but are exact mathematical equivalents linked by Fourier analysis.
To successfully transmit a digital signal over an analog bandpass medium, modulation techniques like ASK, FSK, or PSK must be employed.
A computer network is designed to send information from one point to another.
Information needs to be converted into either a digital or an analog signal for transmission.
Digital transmission is the transmittal of digital signals between two or more points in a communications system.
Digital-to-digital conversion is the representation of digital data by using digital signals.
Digital-to-digital conversion involves three techniques: line coding, block coding, and scrambling.
Line coding is always needed for digital-to-digital conversion.
Block coding and scrambling may or may not be needed in digital-to-digital conversion.
Line coding is the process of converting digital data to digital signals.
Digital data is stored as sequences of bits, such as 0s and 1s, in computer memory.
In line coding, a digital signal is created by assigning different discrete voltage levels to represent data bits.
A data element is the smallest entity that can represent a piece of information, which is the bit.
A signal element is the shortest unit (timewise) of a digital signal.
Data elements are what we need to send; signal elements are what we can send.
Data elements are being carried; signal elements are the carriers.
The ratio 'r' in digital transmission is the number of data elements carried by each signal element.
If each signal element carries one data element, the ratio r is 1.
Data rate defines the number of data elements (bits) sent in one second.
The unit of data rate is bits per second (bps).
Data rate is also commonly referred to as the bit rate.
Signal rate is the number of signal elements sent in one second.
The unit of signal rate is the baud.
Signal rate is also known as the pulse rate, the modulation rate, or the baud rate.
A major goal in data communications is to increase the data rate while decreasing the signal rate.
Increasing the data rate increases the speed of transmission.
Decreasing the signal rate decreases the bandwidth requirement.
The relationship between data rate (N) and signal rate (S) is S = c * N * (1/r).
In the signal rate formula, 'c' is the case factor, which varies from scenario to scenario.
The bandwidth of a nonperiodic digital signal is mathematically continuous with an infinite range.
The effective bandwidth is the finite band that encompasses most of the energy of a digital signal.
The baud rate, not the bit rate, directly determines the required bandwidth for a digital signal.
Baseline wandering occurs when a long string of 0s or 1s alters the receiver's running average of the received signal power.
Baseline wandering makes it difficult for the receiver to correctly evaluate the incoming signal levels.
A DC (direct current) component is created when the voltage level in a digital signal remains constant for a while.
DC components cause problems in systems that cannot pass low frequencies, such as telephone lines or microwave links.
Self-synchronization means that the receiver's clock is precisely aligned with the sender's clock.
To achieve self-synchronization, a digital signal must contain transitions that alert the receiver to the beginning, middle, or end of a pulse.
Built-in error detection capability is a desirable feature in line coding schemes to detect data corruption during transmission.
A good line coding scheme should have a high immunity to noise and interference.
Increasing the number of voltage levels in a signal generally increases the complexity of the transmission system.
Line coding schemes are broadly categorized into unipolar, polar, bipolar, multilevel, and multitransition.
In a unipolar scheme, all the signal levels are on one side of the time axis, either above or below.
Unipolar NRZ (Non-Return-to-Zero) uses a positive voltage for a 1 and zero voltage for a 0.
Unipolar NRZ is called 'non-return-to-zero' because the signal does not return to zero at the middle of the bit.
Unipolar schemes are relatively costly because they consume more power and always contain a DC component.
In polar schemes, the voltages are on both sides of the time axis.
Polar NRZ uses two levels of voltage amplitude.
In Polar NRZ-L (NRZ-Level), the level of the voltage entirely determines the value of the bit.
In Polar NRZ-I (NRZ-Invert), the change or lack of change in the level of the voltage determines the value of the bit.
In NRZ-I, a transition occurs if the next bit is a 1, and no transition occurs if the next bit is a 0.
NRZ-I generally provides better synchronization than NRZ-L when there is a long sequence of 1s.
Both NRZ-L and NRZ-I suffer from baseline wandering and have significant DC components.
Return-to-Zero (RZ) scheme was designed to provide synchronization by using three voltage levels: positive, negative, and zero.
In the RZ scheme, the signal always returns to zero in the middle of each bit interval.
The RZ scheme requires two signal changes to encode a single bit, making it require more bandwidth than NRZ.
Manchester encoding combines the ideas of RZ and NRZ-L.
In Manchester encoding, the duration of the bit is divided into two halves, with a transition always occurring at the middle.
In Manchester encoding, a high-to-low transition represents a 0, and a low-to-high transition represents a 1.
Differential Manchester combines the ideas of RZ and NRZ-I.
In Differential Manchester, there is always a transition at the middle of the bit, but the bit values are determined at the beginning of the bit.
In Differential Manchester, a transition at the start of a bit represents a 0, and no transition represents a 1.
Both Manchester and Differential Manchester overcome baseline wandering and eliminate the DC component.
The required bandwidth for Manchester and Differential Manchester is double that of NRZ.
Bipolar encoding uses three voltage levels: positive, negative, and zero.
In bipolar encoding, the voltage level for one data element is zero, while the voltage level for the other alternates between positive and negative.
Alternate Mark Inversion (AMI) is a common bipolar encoding scheme where the word 'mark' means 1.
In bipolar AMI, a 0 is represented by zero voltage, and a 1 is represented by alternating positive and negative voltages.
Pseudoternary is a bipolar scheme where a 1 is encoded as zero voltage and a 0 is encoded as alternating positive and negative voltages.
The bipolar scheme completely prevents the DC component because the alternating pulses cancel each other out over time.
Multilevel coding schemes are designed to increase the number of bits per baud by encoding a pattern of m data elements into a pattern of n signal elements.
The notation 'mBnL' is often used to describe multilevel coding, where m is the length of the binary pattern, B means binary, n is the length of the signal pattern, and L is the number of levels.
2B1Q (two binary, one quaternary) uses data patterns of size 2 and encodes them into one signal element belonging to a four-level signal.
2B1Q is utilized in Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) technology to provide high-speed internet over telephone lines.
8B6T (eight binary, six ternary) encodes a pattern of 8 bits into a pattern of 6 signal elements using three voltage levels.
8B6T is used in technologies like 100BASE-T4 Fast Ethernet.
4D-PAM5 (four-dimensional five-level pulse amplitude modulation) is a scheme that uses four wires simultaneously.
4D-PAM5 is heavily used in Gigabit Ethernet (1000BASE-T) to transmit data at high speeds over standard twisted-pair cables.
Multitransition coding schemes, such as MLT-3, use a transition to represent a bit value, similar to NRZ-I, but across more than two levels.
MLT-3 (Multiline Transmission, Three Level) uses three levels (+V, 0, -V) and three transition rules to move between the levels.
In MLT-3, if the next bit is 0, there is no transition; if the next bit is 1, the signal transitions to the next state in a sequential order.
Block coding is utilized to improve the performance of line coding by introducing redundancy.
Redundancy added by block coding helps ensure reliable receiver synchronization and allows for error detection.
Block coding changes a block of m bits into a block of n bits, where n is larger than m.
Block coding is often referred to as an mB/nB encoding technique.
Block coding normally involves three steps: division, substitution, and combination.
In the division step of block coding, a sequence of bits is divided into groups of m bits.
In the substitution step, an m-bit group is substituted for an n-bit group.
In the combination step, the n-bit groups are combined together to form a new continuous stream.
The 4B/5B (four binary/five binary) block coding scheme was designed to be used in combination with NRZ-I.
4B/5B solves the synchronization problem of NRZ-I by ensuring that the resulting 5-bit codes do not contain more than three consecutive 0s.
Because 4B/5B uses 5 bits to represent 4 bits, it increases the signal rate and bandwidth requirement by 25%.
In 4B/5B, there are 32 possible 5-bit codes, but only 16 are used for data; the remaining codes are used for control signals or flag errors.
8B/10B (eight binary/ten binary) is a block coding scheme that converts an 8-bit block into a 10-bit block.
The 8B/10B scheme provides greater error detection capability and better synchronization than 4B/5B.
8B/10B is fundamentally a combination of 5B/6B and 3B/4B coding to simplify the substitution hardware.
Bipolar AMI encoding can lose synchronization if a long sequence of 0s is encountered.
Scrambling is a technique used alongside bipolar encoding to substitute long zero-level pulses with a sequence that maintains synchronization.
Unlike block coding, scrambling is done at the same time as the encoding, directly modifying the signal pulses.
B8ZS (Bipolar with 8-Zero Substitution) is a scrambling technique commonly used in North America.
In B8ZS, a sequence of eight consecutive zero-level voltages is replaced by the sequence 000VB0VB.
The 'V' in a scrambling sequence stands for Violation, which is a nonzero voltage that breaks the strict alternating rules of AMI.
The 'B' in a scrambling sequence stands for Bipolar, which is a nonzero voltage in accordance with the AMI alternating rules.
HDB3 (High-Density Bipolar 3-zero) is a scrambling technique commonly used outside of North America.
In HDB3, a sequence of four consecutive zero-level voltages is replaced by either 000V or B00V.
The choice between 000V and B00V in HDB3 depends on the number of nonzero pulses since the last substitution, ensuring the DC component remains zero.
Analog-to-digital conversion refers to the techniques used to translate continuous analog signals into discrete digital data.
Pulse Code Modulation (PCM) is the most common technique used to change an analog signal to digital data.
A PCM encoder performs three distinct processes: sampling, quantizing, and line coding.
Sampling is the first step of PCM, where the continuous analog signal is measured at discrete, equal intervals of time.
The sampling process creates a signal known as Pulse Amplitude Modulation (PAM), which is discrete in time but continuous in amplitude.
The sampling rate, or sampling frequency, dictates how many samples are taken per second.
According to the Nyquist theorem, to accurately reproduce the original analog signal, the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency contained in the signal.
If the analog signal is low-pass, the Nyquist rate is simply twice the bandwidth.
If the analog signal is bandpass, the sampling rate must still be twice the highest frequency, not just twice the bandwidth.
Oversampling occurs when the sampling rate is higher than the Nyquist rate, which is acceptable but uses more bandwidth.
Undersampling occurs when the sampling rate is lower than the Nyquist rate, leading to a distorted reconstruction known as aliasing.
Quantization is the second step of PCM, where the continuous amplitude values of the PAM samples are mapped to discrete levels.
In quantization, the total amplitude range is divided into a set of L intervals, also known as zones.
Each interval is assigned a specific discrete value, often located at the midpoint of the interval.
Quantization error, or quantization noise, is the difference between the original continuous sample value and the assigned discrete value.
Quantization error introduces a persistent noise into the signal that cannot be completely eliminated.
The number of quantization levels (L) directly affects the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio (SNRq).
Increasing the number of quantization levels decreases the quantization error but increases the required data rate.
Non-uniform quantization uses smaller intervals for low-amplitude signals and larger intervals for high-amplitude signals to improve the overall SNRq.
Companding is a practical implementation of non-uniform quantization, where the analog signal is compressed at the source and expanded at the destination.
After quantization, the final step in PCM is encoding, where each quantized level is converted into an n-bit binary code.
The bit rate of a PCM signal can be calculated by multiplying the sampling rate by the number of bits per sample (n).
A classic example of PCM is digitizing voice, where frequencies up to 4000 Hz are sampled at 8000 samples per second.
In standard telephone PCM, each voice sample is quantized into 256 levels, requiring 8 bits per sample, resulting in a 64 kbps bit rate.
The minimum bandwidth of a PCM signal is equal to the bit rate divided by 2.
A PCM decoder reverses the process to recreate the analog signal, first using a digital-to-analog converter to recreate the PAM signal.
After PAM recreation, the decoder passes the signal through a low-pass smoothing filter to recover the original continuous waveform.
Delta Modulation (DM) is an alternative analog-to-digital technique developed to reduce the complexity of PCM.
In DM, the system finds the change from the previous sample rather than recording the absolute value of each sample.
A DM modulator is essentially a 1-bit digitizer that tracks whether the analog signal goes up or down.
If the current analog amplitude is higher than the previous value, the DM modulator outputs a 1.
If the current analog amplitude is lower than the previous value, the DM modulator outputs a 0.
The DM process requires a comparator, a quantizer, and a delay unit holding the previous staircase approximation.
Adaptive Delta Modulation (ADM) improves DM by dynamically changing the step size of the quantization based on the steepness of the signal.
In ADM, the step size increases when the signal changes rapidly and decreases when the signal is relatively flat.
Digital data can be transmitted in two primary modes: parallel and serial.
In parallel transmission, multiple bits are sent simultaneously over multiple wires.
Parallel transmission provides high speed but is costly because it requires n separate physical wires to transmit n bits.
Parallel transmission is typically limited to short distances, such as connecting components inside a computer.
In serial transmission, bits are sent sequentially, one after another, over a single communication channel.
Serial transmission drastically reduces the cost of wiring compared to parallel transmission.
Serial transmission can be divided into three subcategories: asynchronous, synchronous, and isochronous.
In asynchronous transmission, data is sent in discrete groups, usually a byte, without a continuous synchronized clock between sender and receiver.
Asynchronous transmission relies on start bits and stop bits to alert the receiver to the beginning and end of each data byte.
In synchronous transmission, bits are sent in a continuous, unbroken stream without start or stop bits.
Synchronous transmission requires the receiver to accurately count bits and group them into bytes based on timing synchronization.
